title: Weighted Generalization of Nicomachus — Counterexample and Correct Formula
description: Answers the open question from ArithmeticSeriesOQ00: the conjectured identity ∑(2k-1)k² = (∑k)² is FALSE for n ≥ 2. Proves a counterexample at n=2 (LHS=13, RHS=9) and establishes the correct closed form 6∑(2k-1)k² + n(n+1) = n²(n+1)(3n+1).

mathlibDependencies.description: Split last element from range sum for induction

openQuestion: Can we prove the weighted generalization: ∑_{k=1}^n (2k-1)·k² = (∑_{k=1}^n k)²?

overview.historicalContext:
Nicomachus's theorem (c. 100 CE) states that 1³ + 2³ + ⋯ + n³ = (1 + 2 + ⋯ + n)², giving a beautiful identity between sums of cubes and the square of the triangular number. The open question asks whether a weighted version holds: replacing k³ by (2k-1)·k² (the k-th odd number times k²).

The identity (2k-1)·k² reduces to k³ only when 2k-1 = k, i.e., k = 1. For k ≥ 2, the weight (2k-1)k² > k³, making the weighted sum grow faster. Thus the conjectured equality must fail eventually — and it already fails at n=2.
overview.problemStatement: Is ∑_{k=1}^n (2k-1)·k² = (∑_{k=1}^n k)² for all natural numbers n?
overview.proofStrategy: Counterexample at n=2: compute LHS = 1·1² + 3·2² = 1 + 12 = 13 and RHS = (1+2)² = 9. Both are natural number computations, closed by `decide`. For the correct formula, induction on n using `sum_range_succ` with the inductive step closed by `nlinarith` and a ring-proved polynomial identity.
keyInsights: The identity holds at n=1 (both sides = 1), suggesting plausibility; n=2 is the minimal counterexample
The correct formula: 6·∑(2k-1)k² + n(n+1) = n²(n+1)(3n+1), equivalently ∑(2k-1)k² = n(n+1)(3n²+n-1)/6
Nicomachus's theorem ∑k³ = (∑k)² remains true; the weighted version with (2k-1)k² instead of k³ is strictly larger for n≥2
The inductive step identity: n²(n+1)(3n+1) + 6(2n+1)(n+1)² + (n+1)(n+2) - n(n+1) = (n+1)²(n+2)(3n+4), proved by ring

sections.title: Counterexample at n=2
sections.summary: Proves LHS=13 ≠ RHS=9 at n=2 using `decide`. Also shows the identity holds at n=1 and fails again at n=3 (58 ≠ 36).

sections.title: Correct Closed Form
sections.summary: Proves 6∑(2k-1)k² + n(n+1) = n²(n+1)(3n+1) by induction. Spot-checks at n=1,2,3,4 by decide.

sections.title: Contrast with Nicomachus
sections.summary: Restates Nicomachus 4∑k³ = (n(n+1))² and shows ∑k³ ≠ ∑(2k-1)k² for n≥2.

conclusion.summary: The conjectured identity is false for all n ≥ 2. The correct formula 6∑(2k-1)k² + n(n+1) = n²(n+1)(3n+1) is proved by induction with 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: The open question is definitively answered: the weighted generalization with weight (2k-1) does not produce the triangular square. The correct Nicomachus identity uses k³ (not (2k-1)k²) as summands. The difference ∑k³ - ∑(2k-1)k² = ∑k²(1-k) is negative for n≥2.
openQuestions: Is there a weight w(k) other than k² such that ∑w(k)·(2k-1) = (∑k)²? (This would require w(k) = k, giving the trivially true 2∑k² - ∑(2k-1) = ∑(1) = n, not (∑k)².)
Can the Nicomachus identity be generalized to power sums: ∑_{k=1}^n k^r = f(n,r) for some pattern?

crossReferences.description: Directly answers the second open question of ArithmeticSeriesOQ00: the weighted generalization ∑(2k-1)k² = (∑k)² is FALSE.
